claims.text: In CoCrFeMnNi alloys, resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the quality of the pre-formed passive oxide film.
Passive-film thickness, adhesion, and defect density are the key film properties governing tribocorrosion resistance.
Mechanically polished CoCrFeMnNi surfaces have minimal native oxide formation.
Controlled thermal oxidation or anodic polarization can produce CoCrFeMnNi samples with systematically varied passive-film thickness, adhesion, and defect density.
A high-quality passive film acts as a barrier against corrosive attack during mechanical wear.
A high-quality pre-formed film enables rapid repassivation after partial mechanical removal.
A thick, well-adhered, low-defect film can retain its barrier function under moderate wear.
Retention and regeneration of the passive film reduce synergistic degradation from wear and corrosion.
If mechanical film removal outpaces regeneration, degradation accelerates.
Optimized passive-film CoCrFeMnNi samples will have lower overall degradation rates than as-polished or abraded baselines in 3.5 wt% NaCl tribocorrosion tests.
Optimized passive-film samples will show delayed corrosion onset relative to the baseline.
Optimized passive-film samples will show reduced wear rates relative to the baseline.
The passive-film benefit holds only while mechanical wear remains below a critical film-removal threshold.
At extreme wear rates, passive-film removal exceeds regenerative capacity and the protective benefit diminishes.
The prediction may fail at much higher chloride concentrations because the passive film cannot regenerate sufficiently rapidly.
